  • • Availability of resources (Time, Budget, Personnel): Primary data collection requires
  • significant capital, laboratory infrastructure, fieldwork logistics, and time; secondary
  • data is cost-effective, readily retrievable, and efficient (1 mark)
  • • Required precision, control, and data specificity: Primary data allows customized
  • variable control, exact measurement protocols, and high specificity; secondary data
  • may require extensive cleaning and adaptation (1 mark)
  • • Ethical, legal, and accessibility considerations: Availability of public archives
  • institutional clearance, GDPR/data privacy laws, biohazard handling permissions, and

  • square) determine whether differences (e.g., glass refractive indices, soil mineral

  • mark

  • uncertainty, false positive/negative rates adhering to Daubert legal standards — 1
  • mark

  • • Concept of Informed Consent: Voluntary, un-coerced agreement given by a
  • competent participant who has been clearly briefed regarding research aims
  • procedures, anticipated benefits, and potential risks (1 mark)
  • • Participant autonomy and right to withdraw: Respects individual human dignity
  • autonomy, and provides explicit freedom to withdraw participation at any stage
  • without penalty or prejudice (1 mark)
  • • Concept of Confidentiality: Safeguarding participant data, identity, sensitive
  • medical/forensic records, and personal responses from unauthorized access, public
  • disclosure, or third-party misuse (1 mark)
  • • Ethical and Legal Significance: Fosters participant trust, complies with Helsinki
  • Declaration, Institutional Review Board (IRB) mandates, and prevents stigmatization
  • legal hazards, or social harm (1 mark)
  • Question 20. Analyse the major types of probability sampling, namely simple
  • random, systematic, and stratified sampling. Compare their selection
  • procedures and suitability for different population structures. (10 Marks)
  • An]
  • • Concept of Probability Sampling: Core definition wherein every unit in the sampling
  • frame has a known, non-zero chance of selection; enables calculation of sampling
  • error and generalizability of findings (2 marks)
  • • Simple Random Sampling (SRS): Procedure (lottery method, random number
  • generators, equal selection probability P = 1/N); Suitability: Homogeneous, well
  • defined populations with complete sampling frames; Merits and Limitations (free from
  • personal bias; inefficient for widely scattered or heterogeneous populations) — 2.5
  • marks
  • • Systematic Sampling: Procedure (selecting elements at regular intervals through the
  • sampling frame, selecting every k-th element where k = N/n, with random start
  • between 1 and k); Suitability: Ordered, sequential, or production-line datasets; Merits
  • and Limitations (simple, rapid, even spread; high vulnerability to periodicity or hidden
  • cyclical trends in frame) (2.5 marks)
  • • Stratified Sampling: Procedure (dividing heterogeneous population into mutually
  • exclusive, homogeneous sub-groups/strata based on relevant variables like age
  • gender, geographic zone; drawing random samples proportionally or
  • disproportionately from each stratum); Suitability: Highly heterogeneous, diverse
  • populations; Merits and Limitations (highest representativeness, reduces sampling
  • error, allows sub-group analysis; requires detailed prior knowledge of population
  • parameters) (3 marks)
